The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation’s most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong
WASHINGTON -- The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation's most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet reporting Wednesday that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the Defense Department are aware of “a shipment issue" with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters Tuesday. But he denied that the missing parts were “sensitive equipment.”
Australia is one of several nations whose militaries operate the stealth fighter jet.
“Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this,” Marles said.
He added: “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, when Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. The Associated Press sent requests for comment to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after the shipment was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while on the way from Australia to the United States for either repair or disposal months ago. It was not clear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that it prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could have access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has kept tight control over Hong Kong since the territory was returned from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas about 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been made and 19 countries have placed orders for the planes, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.

No. 1 Nebraska volleyball conquers Missouri in straight sets
No. 1 Nebraska volleyball (11-0) finished non-conference play undefeated with a straight-set victory over Missouri (7-5) on Wednesday night (25-10, 25-17, 25-14).
The match was originally scheduled to be played on Sept. 6 at the iconic MLB ballpark, Wrigley Field in Chicago. High humidity and condensation forced officials to suspend the match.
Tonight, the Huskers wore the jerseys they originally planned to wear nearly three weeks ago: white jerseys with red pinstripes — a nod to baseball.
Harper Murray and Andi Jackson each logged 10 kills on a combined 44 swings. Murray hit .241, and Jackson hit a team-high .667 on more than 10 attempts. Additionally, Virginia Adriano matched her season-best with nine kills on 19 attacks.
NU finished hitting .380 in the match, recording 43 kills on 92 swings with only eight attacking errors. An eerie feeling was felt inside the arena, as Teraya Sigler was helped off the court in the second set.
Missouri ended with a season-low .020 hitting percentage with 24 kills and 22 attacking errors.
Set 1: Murray dominates offensively, propels Nebraska
The Huskers stepped onto the floor fueled by fire in the opening set, hitting .448. Murray notched a set-high six kills, averaging 3.03 kills per set this season.
Murray served eight of the nine Husker points on a 9-1 scoring run before Jackson went behind the service line for the final two points, giving Nebraska a 13-4 lead.
Defensively, the Tigers’ 10 points made it the third time this season the Huskers have held their opponents to 10 points or fewer in a set. Missouri hit -.086 and committed nine attacking errors.
Laney Choboy and Sigler each tallied five digs, while Olivia Mauch added four. Bergen Reilly set five different attackers in set one, totaling nine assists.
Set 2: Sigler goes down, Pierce enters
Nebraska jumped into the second set, carrying over momentum from the first. The Big Red hit .303, converting 15 kills. Although the Tigers improved offensively, they recorded a .179 hitting percentage, highlighted by four service errors.
When the Huskers led 16-12, two staff members guided Sigler off the court after she slipped and seemingly injured her right leg. You could hear a pin drop in John Cook Arena as Sigler slowly stood up, walking back toward the Nebraska locker room.
Before leaving the match, the sophomore outside hitter swung nine times without a kill, hitting -.111.
Skyler Pierce entered the match to replace Sigler, but didn’t finish with a promising stat line. The junior recorded two kills and hit .167.
Reilly finished the middle set with a perfect hitting percentage, going 3-for-3 on the attack. The All-American setter totaled five kills, eight digs and 29 assists in the sweep.
Set 3: Jackson explodes for four kills and four blocks
In the final set, without Sigler, the Scarlet and Cream hit .433, notching 13 kills. Jackson contributed four total blocks defensively, holding the Tigers to zero, a very poor attacking clip.
When the Huskers led 11-9, Jackson turned it around and scored four of the next five points for Nebraska. She finished the match with a .667 hitting percentage and two service aces.
Early in the set, Sigler returned to the Husker bench, sitting in street clothes with a boot on her right foot. After the match, head coach Dani Busboom Kelly said she thinks Sigler will be OK but isn’t certain.
Next, the undefeated Huskers begin Big Ten play against Rutgers on Friday, Sept. 25, at 7 p.m. at home. The match will be broadcast on Nebraska Public Media.

Eight US sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy says
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.
The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.
Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran.
The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.
In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew".
He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".
While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.
Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time".
Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable".
"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday.
"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.
The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.
In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.
US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US.
Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.
A study of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.
The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.
Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.

Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.
At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.
In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.
Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing, whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.
Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.
His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry, a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI, and US ties to Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things”.
“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.
The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.
“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.
Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.
On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.
She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.
“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

Ukraine sent two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea, Zelenskiy says
By Tom Balmforth and Brenda Goh
UNITED NATIONS/SEOUL, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," said Zelenskiy in his speech.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die."
Zelenskiy did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January last year. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelenskiy said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told reporters on Thursday that the two North Koreans had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
"While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them," Yu was quoted as saying.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would not be able to confirm the matter, citing the need to protect the safety of the soldiers and their families. The country's Unification Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Korea in June said it would accept all North Korean prisoners of war who fought for Russia and opposed any repatriation of them to Russia or North Korea.
Zelenskiy also criticised North Korea for sending its troops to fight for Russia.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent around 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia's war against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. Most of them have been deployed in the Russian region of Kursk, where they helped Moscow's forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The country has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.
(Reporting by Brenda Goh and Joyce Lee in Seoul and Tom Balmforth in New York; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.title_orig: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation's most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet reporting Wednesday that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the Defense Department are aware of “a shipment issue" with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters Tuesday. But he denied that the missing parts were “sensitive equipment.”
Australia is one of several nations whose militaries operate the stealth fighter jet.
“Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this,” Marles said.
He added: “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, when Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. The Associated Press sent requests for comment to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after the shipment was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while on the way from Australia to the United States for either repair or disposal months ago. It was not clear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that it prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could have access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has kept tight control over Hong Kong since the territory was returned from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas about 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been made and 19 countries have placed orders for the planes, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.
Associated Press writer Didi Tang contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
One of Dolly Parton's sisters is addressing the firing and restraining order against her nephew amid speculation of tension within the family.
She's Alive, LLC (SAL), the entity the late country musician designed to protect her legacy after her Aug. 25 death, filed a lawsuit Sept. 22 alleging her nephew, Bryan Seaver, threatened to smear his aunt’s legacy and made violent threats against several employees. The reported lawsuit and temporary restraining order came a day after Seaver received a termination notice from his role as his late aunt's head of security.
In a brief statement shared on Instagram Sept. 23, Parton's younger sister Freida dismissed the idea of a rift within the family and expressed support for Seaver, her nephew.
"Hi I'll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family. No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly's estate," she wrote. "We all love Bryan, just as we love each other. I love you all!!"
USA TODAY reached out to Seaver through his security company for comment.
Seaver, who oversaw the "Jolene" singer's security operations for more than 20 years, is the son of the late Larry Seaver, who previously held the position, and Dolly's younger sister Cassie Parton, 75.
In addition to working to protect his aunt, her residences and her professional properties, Seaver is the CEO of Squadron Augmented Protection Services, a Nashville-based company offering executive protection, estate security, business intelligence, K-9 services and event security, according to his LinkedIn page.
What is Bryan Seaver accused of?
In a lawsuit filed in Davidson County Chancery Court on Sept. 22, She's Alive LLC (SAL) alleges that Seaver waged a campaign of threats, harassment and intimidation on Parton's family and those entrusted to protect her brand.
Seaver is accused of threatening to ruin Dolly Parton's brand partnerships unless he was paid through podcast appearances and social media, according to the lawsuit obtained by the Nashville Tennesean, part of the USA TODAY Network.
The lawsuit also claimed Seaver made "threats of real-world violence" towards the singer's staff, partners, and legal and business advisers, allegedly often invoking his background as a military contractor during the Iraq War.
"As the entity entrusted by Ms. Parton to protect and promote her life’s work for future generations, SAL must cultivate a safe work environment for employees, advisors, and partners, free from intimidation or hostility — particularly intimidation by an armed former security contractor," the lawsuit reads. "Without relief, Defendants’ calculated campaign will continue to inflict fear, to destabilize SAL’s operations, and to cause further irreparable harm."
The lawsuit said Seaver allegedly told Danny Nozell, the country music legend's former manager who was selected by Parton to run She's Alive, "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or ... pay me."
What has Bryan Seaver said?
In a statement to TMZ shared Sept. 21, Seaver said he and his teams were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions" taken by Nozell and Pinnacle Bank.
"We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much," the statement reads.
Seaver announced his aunt's death in an Aug. 25 video shared on social media, saying he first followed Dolly Parton on the road when he was a kid in the early 1980s and got a taste of the doors she opened for her family "to reach the potential we didn't even know was possible." In the video, he said that Dolly Parton personally asked him to reveal her death.
"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," he said in the video. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not."

articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”
